items.followUp: What is a saturated solution? How can it be changed into an unsaturated solution?

rubric.why: Defines an unsaturated solution by how much solute it contains at a given temperature.
rubric.description: States that the solution contains less than the maximum amount of dissolved solute at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the solution as below its solubility limit at the stated temperature.

rubric.why: Explains how the solution reaches saturation.
rubric.description: Says that adding and dissolving more solute changes it into a saturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the addition of more solute until no more can dissolve.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum amount that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
It can be changed into a saturated solution by adding more solute until no more dissolves at that temperature.

items.followUp: Why does a true solution form a homogeneous mixture?

rubric.why: Identifies the nature and size of suspended particles.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles are relatively large and do not dissolve in the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles are large or insoluble.

rubric.why: Explains why the mixture is not uniform throughout.
rubric.description: States that the particles remain separate, are unevenly distributed or settle, so the mixture is heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the separated or settling particles to the lack of uniformity.

modelAnswer: A suspension does not form a homogeneous mixture because its relatively large particles do not dissolve in the solvent.
The particles remain separate and may settle on standing, so the composition is not uniform throughout; the suspension is heterogeneous.

items.followUp: State three observations from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment and give one limitation of his atomic model.

rubric.why: One key observation was that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: A small number of particles were deflected, showing that positive charge was concentrated in a small region.
rubric.description: States that a few alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: The rare backward scattering showed that the nucleus was very small and dense.
rubric.description: States that very few alpha particles were deflected backward or bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: The model could not account for why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and collapse into the nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives the inability to explain atomic stability as a defect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that orbiting electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, or otherwise stating that atomic stability was unexplained.

rubric.why: The model did not account for the observed line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Gives the inability to explain atomic line spectra as a defect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this defect.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment gave these results:
Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without any deflection.
A few alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected backwards or bounced back.
Two defects of Rutherford’s atomic model were:
It could not explain atomic stability: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: Define a polyatomic ion and give three differences between a molecule and an ion.

rubric.why: Defines a molecular ion as a charged group of bonded atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a molecular ion as a group of atoms bonded together that carries a net charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both the group-of-atoms idea and its charge.

rubric.why: Distinguishes molecules and molecular ions by charge.
rubric.description: States that a molecule is neutral whereas a molecular ion has a charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this paired distinction.

rubric.why: Provides another clear statement of the electrical distinction using suitable terminology.
rubric.description: Correctly contrasts the electrical state of a molecule and a molecular ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a distinct, correctly stated comparison, such as neutral versus charged.

rubric.why: Explains that a molecular ion’s charge results from electron transfer.
rubric.description: States that gaining electrons gives a negative ion or losing electrons gives a positive ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct charge-and-electron relationship.

modelAnswer: A molecular ion is a group of two or more atoms bonded together that carries a net electric charge.
Three differences between a molecule and a molecular ion are:
A molecule is electrically neutral, whereas a molecular ion has a positive or negative charge.
A molecule has no net charge, whereas a molecular ion has a net charge because the group has gained or lost electrons.
A molecular ion is formed when a bonded group of atoms gains electrons (negative charge) or loses electrons (positive charge); a neutral molecule has not gained or lost electrons overall.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of the coordinate covalent bond in the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.

rubric.why: Gives the defining feature of a coordinate covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the one-atom source of the shared pair.

rubric.why: Identifies how the donating atom supplies the shared pair.
rubric.description: States that the donor atom uses a lone pair of electrons to form the bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the donor’s lone pair.

rubric.why: Identifies the atoms/ions participating in the standard ammonium-ion example.
rubric.description: Identifies ammonia and a hydrogen ion as the reactants in the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming or writing the reactants.

rubric.why: Shows the correct formation of the ammonium ion.
rubric.description: Writes or states the formation of NH₄⁺ from NH₃ and H⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation or equivalent statement.

rubric.why: Explains which atom donates the pair and how it bonds to the acceptor.
rubric.description: Explains that nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺, which has no electron to contribute to the shared pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the donation and bond formation.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
The atom that donates the pair has a lone pair of electrons; the atom receiving it has an electron deficiency.
For example, ammonia has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom, and a hydrogen ion can accept this pair.
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form a coordinate covalent bond in the ammonium ion.

items.followUp: Write balanced equations for the reactions of sodium with water, oxygen, hydrogen and chlorine.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with water.
rubric.description: Writes the equation forming sodium hydroxide and hydrogen from sodium and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct, balanced equation.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with oxygen.
rubric.description: Writes the equation forming sodium oxide from sodium and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct, balanced equation.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with hydrogen.
rubric.description: Writes the equation forming sodium hydride from sodium and hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct, balanced equation.

rubric.why: Tests the balanced equation for sodium reacting with chlorine.
rubric.description: Writes the equation forming sodium chloride from sodium and chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct, balanced equation.

modelAnswer: With water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
With oxygen: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
With hydrogen: 2Na + H₂ → 2NaH
With chlorine: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

items.followUp: Write the empirical formulae of ethene and glucose.

rubric.why: Tests the empirical formula of silica.
rubric.description: Gives SiO₂ as the empirical formula of silica.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Tests the simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen in benzene.
rubric.description: Gives CH as the empirical formula of benzene.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

modelAnswer: The empirical formula of silica is SiO₂.
The empirical formula of benzene is CH.

items.followUp: Define a diatomic molecule and give one example.

rubric.why: Tests the number of atoms in a triatomic molecule.
rubric.description: Defines a triatomic molecule as one containing three atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains three atoms.

rubric.why: Tests recognition of a valid triatomic example.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as H₂O, CO₂ or O₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A triatomic molecule is a molecule that contains three atoms.
For example, a water molecule (H₂O) is triatomic.
